### Problem: Rank Transform of an Array {#sec-srt-p4-a}

::: {.p-statement}
An array `arr` ($0 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^9 \le \mathit{arr}[i] \le 10^9$). Replace each element with its **rank**: ranks start at $1$, larger values get larger ranks, equal values share a rank, and ranks are as small as possible. Return the transformed array.

Source: [LC 1331 · Rank Transform of an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/rank-transform-of-an-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}

Example: `arr = [40,10,20,30]` → `[4,1,2,3]`; `arr = [100,100,100]` → `[1,1,1]`; `arr = [37,12,28,9,100,56,80,5,12]` → `[5,3,4,2,8,6,7,1,3]`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A rank is "how many *distinct* values are strictly smaller, plus one." The moment you see that, the problem is **coordinate compression**: replace a huge, sparse value (up to $10^9$) by its dense index in the sorted list of distinct values — exactly what @sec-srt-a4 promises in one line. Build `sorted(set(arr))`; the position of each value there (1-based) is its rank. Look it up per element and you are done in $O(n\log n)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Count the smaller ones, per element.** For each value, rank $= 1 + |\{u \in \text{distinct values} : u < v\}|$. $O(n^2)$ time — a direct reading of the definition, and the oracle.
2. **Sort the distinct values once, `bisect_left` per element.** Same definition, but sorted *once* up front so each rank query is a $O(\log n)$ binary search on the sorted distinct list instead of a fresh $O(n)$ scan. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.
3. **Coordinate compression via `sorted(set)` + a dict.** Sort the distinct values once; make a dictionary mapping value $\to$ its 1-based position; map every element through it. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space, but the per-element cost drops from $\log n$ to $O(1)$ and the whole thing fits in two lines.

**Invariant.** After `rank = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(arr)))}`, `rank[v]` equals $1 +$ (number of distinct values below $v$) for every present $v$, because the sorted distinct list places exactly that many values before it — which is precisely the required rank.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Count the distinct smaller values

::: {.form-next}
Translate the definition literally: an element's rank is one plus the number of *distinct* values strictly smaller than it. For each position, count those. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(n)$ space (the distinct set) — slow, but it states the rule and checks the fast form.

**Worked example.** `arr = [40,10,20,30]`, distinct $= \{10,20,30,40\}$. For $40$ there are $3$ distinct values smaller → rank $4$. For $10$, none smaller → rank $1$. For $20$, one ($10$) → rank $2$. For $30$, two ($10,20$) → rank $3$. Result $[4,1,2,3]$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("rank", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "[4, 1, 2, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def rank_scan(arr):
    uniq = set(arr)
    return [1 + sum(1 for u in uniq if u < v) for v in arr]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - per-element count (O(n^2) oracle)
#include <vector>
#include <set>
using namespace std;
vector<int> rankScan(vector<int> arr) {
    set<int> uniq(arr.begin(), arr.end());
    vector<int> out;
    for (int v : arr) {
        int r = 1;
        for (int u : uniq) if (u < v) ++r;
        out.push_back(r);
    }
    return out;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `uniq = set(arr)` collapses duplicates so equal values rank the same. `1 + sum(1 for u in uniq if u < v)` counts distinct values strictly below `v` and adds one — the definition of rank. List-comp over `arr` preserves original order and repeats. Nothing is sorted globally; each element re-scans the distinct set, hence $O(n \cdot |\text{uniq}|)$.

#### Sort the distinct list, bisect per element

::: {.form-next}
The count-per-element rung rescans the whole distinct set for every element. Fix that by sorting the distinct list *once*, then reading each rank as a binary-search position — `bisect_left(uniq, v)` returns how many distinct values are strictly below $v$, so rank is one more. Same $O(n\log n)$ total as form 3 below, but $\log n$ per element instead of $O(1)$ dict lookup, and no auxiliary map. It earns its place by showing exactly what compression will later buy: **turning an $O(\log n)$ query into $O(1)$ costs only a hash table.**

**`bisect_left`, in plain words.** In a sorted list, `bisect_left(uniq, v)` returns the index where `v` would be inserted to keep the list sorted, scanning from the left of any equal run. When `v` is *present* in `uniq`, that index equals the number of strictly smaller elements — exactly our rank-minus-one. So rank is `bisect_left(...) + 1`.

**Worked example.** `arr = [40, 10, 20, 30]` gives `uniq = [10, 20, 30, 40]`. `bisect_left(uniq, 40) = 3` → rank 4; `= 0` for 10 → rank 1; `= 1` for 20 → rank 2; `= 2` for 30 → rank 3. Result $[4, 1, 2, 3]$ — the same as the brute count, at $O(\log n)$ per lookup instead of $O(n)$.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]

    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("rank", "bisect")
    assert str(final) == "[4, 1, 2, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1331-bisect
def rank_bisect(arr):
    uniq = sorted(set(arr))
    return [bisect.bisect_left(uniq, v) + 1 for v in arr]

for _ in range(300):
    arr = [random.randint(-20, 20) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 12))]
    assert rank_bisect(arr) == rank_scan(arr)
assert rank_bisect([40, 10, 20, 30]) == [4, 1, 2, 3]
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

vector<int> arrayRankTransformBisect(vector<int> arr) {
    vector<int> u = arr;
    sort(u.begin(), u.end());
    u.erase(unique(u.begin(), u.end()), u.end());
    for (int& x : arr) x = (int)(lower_bound(u.begin(), u.end(), x) - u.begin()) + 1;
    return arr;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{40, 10, 20, 30}; arrayRankTransformBisect(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `uniq = sorted(set(arr))` is the same sorted distinct list the compression rung builds. `bisect.bisect_left(uniq, v) + 1` reads rank as position — one binary search, $O(\log n)$, instead of the $O(n)$ `sum(1 for u in uniq if u < v)` scan. In C++ `lower_bound(u.begin(), u.end(), x) - u.begin()` is the same `bisect_left`; the surrounding `sort` + `unique` + `erase` idiom produces the sorted distinct vector. Overall: $O(n\log n)$, dominated by either the initial sort or the $n$ binary searches (they are the same order).

#### Coordinate compression: sorted(set), then one dict

::: {.form-next}
Sort the distinct values and let a value's **1-based index** be its rank. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. This is the canonical coordinate-compression idiom — the "in one line" of @sec-srt-a4 — and it recurs across the whole arrays volume whenever values are sparse but only their *relative order* matters. Compared to the bisect rung, one dictionary pass replaces every $\log n$ binary search with an $O(1)$ hash lookup; the sort is the same, the code is shorter.

**Coordinate compression, in plain words.** When only the *ranking* of values matters (not their magnitudes), you replace each value by its position in the sorted list of distinct values. Big numbers ($10^9$) become small dense indices ($1 \dots n$), so arrays, hash keys, or segment trees can be sized by $n$ instead of by the value range. The recipe is always `sorted(set(...))` plus a dictionary from value to index — a sort (the expensive part) and an $O(1)$ lookup per element.

**Worked example.** `arr = [37,12,28,9,100,56,80,5,12]`. `sorted(set) = [5,9,12,28,37,56,80,100]`, so rank map $5{:}1, 9{:}2, 12{:}3, 28{:}4, 37{:}5, 56{:}6, 80{:}7, 100{:}8$. Mapping each element: $[5,3,4,2,8,6,7,1,3]$ — equal $12$'s share rank $3$, exactly LC's third example.
:::

```{python}

    assert str(final) == "[4, 1, 2, 3]"

V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1331-compress
def rank_compress(arr):
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(arr)))}
    return [rank[v] for v in arr]

for _ in range(300):
    arr = [random.randint(-20, 20) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 12))]
    assert rank_compress(arr) == rank_scan(arr)
assert rank_compress([40, 10, 20, 30]) == [4, 1, 2, 3]                 # LC example
assert rank_compress([100, 100, 100]) == [1, 1, 1]                     # all equal
assert rank_compress([37, 12, 28, 9, 100, 56, 80, 5, 12]) == [5, 3, 4, 2, 8, 6, 7, 1, 3]
assert rank_compress([]) == []                                          # empty is legal
print("rank_compress OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <unordered_map>
using namespace std;

vector<int> arrayRankTransform(vector<int> arr) {
    vector<int> u = arr;
    sort(u.begin(), u.end());
    u.erase(unique(u.begin(), u.end()), u.end());     // sorted distinct values
    unordered_map<int, int> rank;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)u.size(); ++i) rank[u[i]] = i + 1;
    for (int& x : arr) x = rank[x];
    return arr;
}

int main() { vector<int> v{40, 10, 20, 30}; arrayRankTransform(v); }
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `sorted(set(arr))` is the distinct values in order — `set` collapses duplicates (equal ranks), `sorted` assigns increasing positions. `{v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(...)}` turns that order into a value→rank dictionary (1-based, so ranks "start from 1"). `[rank[v] for v in arr]` maps every element, preserving order and duplicates. In C++ the same three moves: copy+`sort`, `unique` (with the erase idiom) to dedup, build the map, then overwrite each element with its rank.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Count-per-element** is $O(n^2)$ time. **Bisect on the sorted distinct list** is $O(n\log n)$ time — one sort and $n$ binary searches — with $O(n)$ space for the distinct array. **Dict-based compression** is $O(n\log n)$ time (the sort) and $O(n)$ space (set + dict), with $O(1)$ rank lookup per element. Compression is the reusable prize, not just this answer: any time a problem mentions order/rank but values reach $10^9$, map them to $1 \dots n$ first, then index arrays or trees by that dense range (@sec-lang-p3-frequency sorts by a *derived* count instead — the same "sort on a computed key" family).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 0$: `sorted(set([]))` is empty, map is empty, result `[]` — guard not needed but tested.
- Negative and duplicate values: `set` handles duplicates (shared rank); sorting handles negatives naturally.
- Value range $10^9$ rules out a value-indexed histogram — the failure mode spelled out for @sec-srt-p3-b; compression by *rank* is the workaround.
:::
